questions.question_text:
Find $E(X)$ for the distribution below.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.3 & 0.25 & 0.35 & 0.1 \end{array}$

options.why: Averaged the four values and ignored the probabilities.
Gave the most likely value, the one with the largest probability, instead of the mean.
Divided the weighted total by $4$, averaging a second time.

questions.question_text: A distribution is given by the ordered pairs $(2,\ 0.45)$, $(5,\ 0.1)$, $(9,\ 0.3)$, $(12,\ 0.15)$. Find $E(X)$.

options.why: Averaged the four values without weighting them by their probabilities.
Gave the value with the largest probability instead of the expected value.
Added the four values and never multiplied by the probabilities.

questions.question_text: A random variable has $P(x)=\frac{x+1}{15}$ for $x \in \{1,\ 2,\ 3,\ 5\}$. Find $E(X)$.

options.why: Averaged the four values $1$, $2$, $3$ and $5$ without using the probabilities.
Gave the value with the largest probability rather than the weighted mean.
Inverted the final fraction, dividing $15$ by $50$ instead of $50$ by $15$.

questions.question_text:
Find $E(X)$ for the distribution below.
$\begin{array}{c|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.22 & m & 0.31 & 0.17 \end{array}$

options.why: Took $m$ to be $0.7$, the total of the three known probabilities, instead of $1-0.7$.
Left the unknown column out of the sum instead of finding $m$ first.
Averaged the values $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$ and ignored the probabilities.

questions.question_text: For $X$, the number of passengers in a car passing a checkpoint, $E(X)=1.68$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Over a large number of cars, the average number of passengers per car is about $1.68$.
The most common number of passengers in a car is about $1.68$.
options.why: Confused the expected value with the mode, the value of highest probability.

options.text: The value $1.68$ is impossible, so $E(X)$ has been calculated incorrectly.
options.why: Assumed the expected value must be one of the values $X$ can take.

options.text: Every car passing the checkpoint carries $1.68$ passengers.
options.why: Read the mean as the result of a single trial rather than a long-run average.

questions.solution_text:
The expected value is the long-run average of $X$.
Over a large number of cars, the average number of passengers per car is about $1.68$.

questions.question_text: A drawer holds $7$ batteries, of which $3$ are flat. Two batteries are taken at random without replacement. Let $X$ be the number of flat batteries taken. Find $E(X)$.

options.why: Counted only one order for exactly one flat battery, so $P(X=1)$ was halved.
Gave the probability that a single battery is flat instead of the expected number.
Rounded the expected value to a whole number, assuming $E(X)$ must be a possible value of $X$.

questions.question_text: The random variable $X$ takes the values $2$, $4$ and $6$ with $P(X=2)=0.5$, $P(X=4)=t$ and $P(X=6)=u$. Given that $E(X)=3.6$, find $u$.

options.why: Solved the pair of equations correctly but reported $t$ instead of $u$.
Split the remaining $0.5$ equally between the two unknowns without using $E(X)$.
Solved $2u=0.6$ by reading off the right-hand side instead of halving it.

questions.question_text:
Find $E(X)$ for the distribution below.
$\begin{array}{c|ccccc} x & -5 & -2 & 0 & 3 & 8 \\ \hline P(X=x) & 0.2 & 0.25 & 0.15 & 0.3 & 0.1 \end{array}$

options.why: Ignored the negative signs when multiplying the first two values.
Left the two negative terms out of the sum altogether.
Computed both totals correctly but subtracted the positive total from the negative one.
